name: TLV75712PDBVR
title: TLV757P 1 A low-IQ low-dropout regulator, fixed outputs 0.6 V to 5 V
summary: The TLV757P is a 1 A PMOS low-dropout linear regulator with fixed output voltages from 0.6 V to 5 V, an input range of 1.45 V to 5.5 V and 25 µA typical ground current. Output accuracy is ±1 % from –40 °C to 85 °C, and dropout at 1 A is 425 mV maximum for 3.3 V parts. It has an enable input, built-in soft-start, foldback current limit, thermal shutdown, undervoltage lockout and an active pulldown that discharges the output when off, and a single 1 µF ceramic capacitor on the output keeps it stable. It comes in the 5-pin SOT-23 (DBV), the 5-pin SOT-23 with thermal pad (DYD) and the 2 mm × 2 mm 6-pin WSON (DRV); TLV75712PDBVR is the 1.2 V part in DBV.
key_figures: 1000 mV typ, 1050 mV max (1.2 V ≤ VOUT < 1.5 V, –40 °C to 85 °C); 300 mV typ, 425 mV max (3.3 V ≤ VOUT < 5 V)

circuits.title: Post-regulating a DC-DC converter
circuits.description: A DC-DC converter supplies IN through a 1 µF capacitor to ground; the regulated OUT feeds the load across a second 1 µF capacitor. EN is brought out as an on/off control. The worked design takes 2.5 V in, delivers 1.8 V at 600 mA DC, and allows up to 70 °C ambient.
notes: With RθJA = 100.2 °C/W, 0.7 V across the regulator and 0.6 A, the junction stays at or below 125 °C up to an ambient of 82.916 °C.

circuits.title: Reverse-current protection with a Schottky diode
circuits.description: A Schottky diode sits across the regulator with its anode on OUT and its cathode on IN, in parallel with the pass transistor's internal body diode. When the output is pushed above the input, current flows through the Schottky rather than the body diode. CIN and COUT go from IN and OUT to ground.
notes: The protection involves only the regulator's IN, OUT and GND pins.

operation.text: A 1 A PMOS low-dropout regulator with fixed output voltages from 0.6 V to 5 V in 50 mV steps, a 1.45 V to 5.5 V input range and 25 µA typical quiescent current. It has soft-start, foldback current limit, thermal shutdown, undervoltage lockout and an active output pulldown when off. A 1 µF ceramic capacitor on OUT is enough for stability. Junction operating range is –40 °C to +125 °C.

The output voltage is set by an internal divider; its lower resistor R2 is 550 kΩ and the upper resistor R1 differs from one output voltage to the next. A 120 Ω switch from OUT to GND provides the output pulldown.
Below the rising UVLO threshold (VUVLO, 1.3 V typical) the output stays off and is tied to ground through the 120 Ω pulldown. The falling threshold is about 40 mV lower.

EN is active high: above VHI (1 V minimum) the device turns on, below VLO (0.3 V maximum) it turns off. EN may be tied to IN when no shutdown is needed. EN works independently of IN, but when EN sits above VIN the EN pin current rises; in that case either bring EN up after VIN, tie EN to VIN, or keep the EN toggle rate below 10 kHz.

Every TLV757P (the P in the part number) pulls OUT to ground through about 120 Ω when disabled, so the output falls with the time constant set by COUT and the load in parallel with the pulldown. The pulldown works only while enough input voltage is present. RPULLDOWN is 95 Ω typical at VIN = 3.3 V.
An internal soft-start ramps the output monotonically, limiting inrush current into the output capacitor and the dip on the input during start-up. Typical start-up time is 550 µs.

The limit is a fixed (brick-wall) current until the output falls below 0.4 × VOUT(NOM); below that the allowed current folds back as the output approaches ground, reaching ISC (755 mA typical) into a short. In current limit the output is not regulated: it equals the limited current times the load resistance. In a short the pass transistor dissipates (VIN – VOUT) × ISC until thermal shutdown trips; after cooling the device restarts, and it goes on alternating between limiting and thermal trips for as long as the fault lasts.

During start-up the foldback limit holds the current below the minimum ICL. A constant-current load, or an output held negative at enable, can ask for more than the foldback limit allows, and the output may then not reach its full value; keep a constant-current load disconnected until the output is up. Too much inductance in the output path makes the current limit oscillate during a fault.

The output turns off when the junction reaches about 165 °C and back on at about 155 °C, so under sustained overload the device cycles on and off. Junction temperature should be held at 125 °C or below for reliable operation; repeatedly running into thermal shutdown wears the device. To check thermal margin, raise the ambient temperature with the worst-case load until the protection trips.
The output regulates when VIN exceeds VOUT(NOM) + VDO, EN has risen past its rising threshold and has not since dropped below its falling threshold, IOUT is below ICL, and TJ is below TSD.

With VIN below VOUT(NOM) + VDO and everything else normal, the pass transistor is fully on (in its linear, resistive region) and the output follows the input; load and line transients then cause large output swings. Coming out of steady dropout, the loop has been driving the pass transistor as hard as it can, so the output overshoots VOUT(NOM) on a fast input step until regulation returns.
With EN below VLO the pass transistor and internal circuits are off and the output is discharged to ground by the internal switch.

Stability needs at least 0.47 µF of effective output capacitance; X5R or X7R ceramics hold their value and ESR best over temperature. Allow for DC-bias loss, which grows with output voltage: plan on ceramics losing half their value. Output capacitance of 200 µF or less gives the best performance. Put at least 1 µF on IN. A high-impedance or reactive source needs more input capacitance, several in parallel if the impedance is high over a wide frequency range; a larger input capacitor also helps with large, fast load steps or when the regulator sits several inches from its source.

Once in dropout the PMOS pass device acts as a resistor, its RDS(on), between IN and OUT, so dropout voltage rises in proportion to output current. PSRR and transient response worsen as VIN – VOUT approaches dropout.

A slowly ramping input at start-up holds the regulator in dropout, and the output overshoots when it regains regulation; starting with EN rather than with the input ramp avoids this. A line step out of dropout also overshoots, because the error amplifier must pull the pass-transistor gate back from fully on; more input capacitance slows the step and reduces the overshoot.

Current forced from OUT to IN goes through the pass transistor's body diode and, if large, harms long-term reliability through electromigration, heating or latch-up. It happens when a large COUT holds the output up while the input collapses at light load, when the output is driven before the input is present, or when the output is driven above the input; all of these break the VOUT ≤ VIN + 0.3 V rating. Where it is expected, add external protection such as a Schottky diode from OUT to IN.

Dissipation is roughly (VIN – VOUT) × IOUT, so the input rail should sit as close above the output as dropout allows. Heat leaves mainly through the thermal pad, which should be soldered to a copper area with an array of plated vias to inner or bottom-side planes, away from other hot parts. RθJA depends strongly on the board's copper area, weight and plane placement and is useful mainly to compare packages; ψJT and ψJB give a junction estimate from a measured top or board temperature that depends little on copper area.
In steady operation the input current is about equal to the output current; at start-up it is higher by the current charging the output capacitor.
IN should be fed from a low-impedance supply. A reactive source calls for extra capacitors alongside the 1 µF one on IN, to keep the supply impedance low across frequency.

Place CIN and COUT as close to the device as possible, use copper planes for the device connections, and add thermal vias around the device. On the DYD and DRV packages solder the thermal pad to copper; leaving it unsoldered raises thermal resistance a great deal.

TLV757xx(x)Pyyyz: xx(x) is the output voltage, two digits for voltages on a 50 mV grid and three otherwise (28 = 2.8 V, 125 = 1.25 V); P marks the active output discharge, which every TLV757P has; yyy is the package (DBV, DYD, DRV); z is the packing, R for a 3000-piece reel and T for 250-piece tape. Output voltages from 0.6 V to 5 V in 50 mV steps are offered on request.
